headings.text: Polar form of a complex number
Multiplication and division in polar form

html:
The big picture

x^2 + 1 = 0 has no real solution, so the number system is enlarged once more: add an imaginary unit i with i^2 = -1, and every complex number is z = a + bi with real part a and imaginary part b. Each complex number is a point (or arrow) in the complex plane, and that picture explains the rules. Addition is vector addition. Multiplication is clumsy in Cartesian form but simple in polar form z = r(\cos\varphi + i\sin\varphi) = re^{i\varphi} (Euler's formula): multiply the moduli r, add the arguments \varphi. Division works by multiplying with the complex conjugate \bar z, because z\bar z = \lvert z\rvert^2 is real. Powers follow from polar multiplication (De Moivre's formula), and the equation w^n = z has exactly n n-th roots, spaced evenly on a circle. The fundamental theorem of algebra completes the story: over \mathbb{C}, every polynomial of degree n has exactly n roots counted with multiplicity. Engineers use all of this because one complex number stores an amplitude and a phase, which turns AC-circuit and oscillation problems into algebra.

Why complex numbers?

Real numbers solve many equations, but not all polynomial equations. Over \mathbb{R},

x^2 + 1 = 0

has no solution, because x^2 \ge 0. Introduce a number i with

i^2 = -1.

Then x^2 + 1 = 0 \implies x = \pm i. \mathbb{R} \subset \mathbb{C}: we enlarge the number system once again.

Board. The equation x^2 = -1 has no real solution. Introduce i^2 = -1, x = \pm i. The whole chain: \mathbb{N} \subset \mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{R} \subset \mathbb{C}.

Symbols
  • x — the unknown (first a real number, then allowed to be complex)
  • i — the imaginary unit, a new number defined by i^2 = -1
  • \mathbb{R} — the real numbers; \mathbb{C} — the complex numbers; \subset — "is a subset of"
Connection

Same pattern as in 3 Set of Real Numbers: each number system \mathbb{N} \subseteq \mathbb{Z} \subseteq \mathbb{Q} \subseteq \mathbb{R} was built to solve equations the previous one couldn't (x + 1 = 0, 2x = 1, x^2 = 2). \mathbb{C} is the next and last step: after it, every polynomial equation has a solution (see Fundamental theorem of algebra).

Where engineers meet complex numbers

Oscillations and waves:

  • AC circuits and impedance;
  • signal processing and Fourier analysis;
  • control systems and frequency response;
  • electromagnetism and wave propagation.

Why they help:

  • one number stores amplitude and phase;
  • rotations become multiplication;
  • sinusoidal calculations become algebraic;
  • polynomial equations have a complete root theory.

We return to a simple AC-circuit example after polar form.

Definition and notation

A complex number has the form

z = a + bi, \qquad a, b \in \mathbb{R}, \qquad i^2 = -1,

with real part \operatorname{Re}(z) = a and imaginary part \operatorname{Im}(z) = b.

Symbols
  • z — a complex number
  • a = \operatorname{Re}(z) — its real part, a real number
  • b = \operatorname{Im}(z) — its imaginary part, also a real number (the coefficient of i, not bi)
  • i — the imaginary unit, i^2 = -1
  • Real numbers are included: a = a + 0i.
  • Example: z = 2 + 3i, so \operatorname{Re}(z) = 2, \operatorname{Im}(z) = 3.

Board. Real numbers inside \mathbb{C}: z = a + 0i = a. z = 0 + bi is purely imaginary when b \neq 0. Examples: z = 4: \operatorname{Re} z = 4, \operatorname{Im} z = 0. z = -3i: \operatorname{Re} z = 0, \operatorname{Im} z = -3.

  • Equality is componentwise:
a + bi = c + di \iff a = c \text{ and } b = d.
Symbols
  • a, b, c, d \in \mathbb{R} — real and imaginary parts of the two complex numbers being compared
Common mistake — \operatorname{Im}(z) is real

For z = 2 + 3i it's tempting to write \operatorname{Im}(z) = 3i. But the imaginary part is the real coefficient 3; the i only marks which part it is. This matters as soon as you compute with it: \lvert z\rvert = \sqrt{\operatorname{Re}(z)^2 + \operatorname{Im}(z)^2} = \sqrt{4 + 9}, whereas with "3i" you would get \sqrt{4 + (3i)^2} = \sqrt{-5}, which is nonsense.

Quick check: powers of i

What happens when we keep multiplying by i?

i^1 = i, \qquad i^2 = -1, \qquad i^3 = -i, \qquad i^4 = 1.

The powers repeat with period 4. (The slide draws the four values on a circle: i at the top, -1 left, -i bottom, 1 right.)

Board. i^2 = -1, i^3 = -i, i^4 = 1, i^{2026} = -1. The powers repeat every four steps.

Intuition — multiplying by i is a quarter turn

Follow the four values in the plane: 1 \to i \to -1 \to -i \to 1 is a walk around the circle in steps of 90^\circ anticlockwise. So "multiply by i" means "rotate by 90^\circ", and i^2 = -1 is just two quarter turns = a half turn, which flips 1 to -1. This is the cleanest way to see that i is not mysterious: it's a rotation. To get any power, reduce the exponent mod 4: i^{27} = i^{24} \cdot i^3 = 1 \cdot (-i) = -i.

The complex plane

A complex number z = a + bi can be viewed as

  • the point (a, b);
  • the vector from the origin to (a, b).

The horizontal axis is the real axis; the vertical axis is the imaginary axis.

Board. The complex plane is also called the Argand plane. \operatorname{Re} z is measured along the horizontal axis, \operatorname{Im} z along the vertical axis: z = 3 + 2i \leftrightarrow (3, 2), and (a, b) \neq (b, a) in general.

Addition is vector addition

Let z_1 = 2 + i, z_2 = 1 + 2i. Then z_1 + z_2 = 3 + 3i.

z_1 + z_2 is the diagonal of the parallelogram spanned by z_1 and z_2.

Board: addition and subtraction. For z_1 = a_1 + b_1 i and z_2 = a_2 + b_2 i: z_1 + z_2 = (a_1 + a_2) + i(b_1 + b_2), z_1 - z_2 = (a_1 - a_2) + i(b_1 - b_2). Example with the same z_1 = 2 + i, z_2 = 1 + 2i: z_1 + z_2 = (2 + 1) + (1 + 2)i = 3 + 3i, z_1 - z_2 = (2 - 1) + (1 - 2)i = 1 - i. Geometrically, addition follows the parallelogram rule.

Connection

This is exactly the tip-to-tail rule for vectors in \mathbb{R}^2 from 2.1 Linear Algebra Fundamentals: as far as addition is concerned, \mathbb{C} is the plane \mathbb{R}^2. What's new is multiplication, which vectors in \mathbb{R}^2 don't have.

Multiplication in Cartesian form

For z_1 = a + bi, z_2 = c + di:

z_1 z_2 = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i.
Symbols
  • z_1 = a + bi, z_2 = c + di — the two factors; a, b, c, d \in \mathbb{R}
  • ac - bd — real part of the product (the -bd comes from bi \cdot di = bd\,i^2 = -bd)
  • ad + bc — imaginary part of the product

Example:

(2 + i)(1 - 3i) = 2 - 6i + i - 3i^2 = 5 - 5i.

Use ordinary algebra, then replace i^2 by -1.

Board. If z_1 = a + bi and z_2 = c + di, use i^2 = -1: z_1 z_2 = (a + bi)(c + di) = ac + adi + bci + bdi^2 = (ac - bd) + i(ad + bc). Reminder: collect real parts and imaginary parts separately.

Common mistake — the sign of bd

Multiplying out (a + bi)(c + di) gives four terms, and the last one is bd\,i^2 = -bd. Forgetting the minus (writing ac + bd) is the most common error. Check with the slide's example: (2 + i)(1 - 3i) has b d = 1 \cdot (-3) = -3, so the real part is 2 - (-3) = 5, not 2 + (-3) = -1.

Conjugate and modulus

For z = x + yi, define

\bar z = x - yi, \qquad \lvert z\rvert = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}.
Symbols
  • z = x + yi — a complex number with real part x and imaginary part y
  • \bar z — the complex conjugate of z: same real part, imaginary part with the opposite sign
  • \lvert z\rvert — the modulus (absolute value) of z: a real number \ge 0

Geometry:

  • \bar z is the reflection of z across the real axis;
  • \lvert z\rvert is the distance from z to the origin.

Board. \operatorname{Re} \bar z = \operatorname{Re} z, \operatorname{Im} \bar z = -\operatorname{Im} z. Examples: if z = 3 + 4i, then \bar z = 3 - 4i, \lvert z\rvert = 5. If z = -1 - \sqrt3\,i, then \lvert z\rvert = 2. Conjugation reflects a point in the real axis.

Connection

For a real number (y = 0) the modulus is \sqrt{x^2} = \lvert x\rvert, the absolute value from 3 Set of Real Numbers. So \lvert z\rvert is the natural extension, and \lvert z_1 - z_2\rvert is the distance between two points in the plane, just as \lvert x - a\rvert was the distance on the line.

Useful conjugate identities

z\bar z = \lvert z\rvert^2, \qquad \overline{z_1 + z_2} = \bar z_1 + \bar z_2, \qquad \overline{z_1 z_2} = \bar z_1\,\bar z_2,
\operatorname{Re} z = \frac{z + \bar z}{2}, \qquad \operatorname{Im} z = \frac{z - \bar z}{2i}, \qquad \lvert z_1 z_2\rvert = \lvert z_1\rvert\,\lvert z_2\rvert.
Symbols
  • z, z_1, z_2 — complex numbers; \bar z etc. their conjugates; \lvert\cdot\rvert the modulus
  • \overline{z_1 + z_2} — the conjugate of the sum (the bar over the whole expression)

The identity z\bar z = \lvert z\rvert^2 is the key to division.

Board. One more identity: \lvert z\rvert^2 = (\operatorname{Re} z)^2 + (\operatorname{Im} z)^2.

Why is z\bar z always real?

Multiply out: (x + yi)(x - yi) = x^2 - xyi + xyi - y^2 i^2 = x^2 + y^2. The two imaginary terms cancel and -y^2 i^2 = +y^2. So z\bar z is a real number, and it equals \lvert z\rvert^2. This is the same trick as "multiply by the conjugate surd" from school ((a + \sqrt b)(a - \sqrt b) = a^2 - b), and it is why division works: it turns a complex denominator into a real one.

Common mistake — \lvert z\rvert^2 \ne z^2

For real numbers \lvert x\rvert^2 = x^2, so it's tempting to compute \lvert z\rvert^2 as z^2. For complex z these differ: z = 1 + i gives z^2 = 1 + 2i - 1 = 2i (not even real), while \lvert z\rvert^2 = z\bar z = 1 + 1 = 2. The square of the modulus needs the conjugate.

Reciprocal and division

For z = a + bi \ne 0, multiply numerator and denominator by \bar z = a - bi:

\frac{1}{z} = \frac{1}{a + bi} \cdot \frac{a - bi}{a - bi} = \frac{a - bi}{a^2 + b^2}, \qquad \text{i.e.} \qquad \frac{1}{z} = \frac{\bar z}{\lvert z\rvert^2} \quad (z \ne 0).
Symbols
  • z = a + bi \ne 0 — the number being inverted; \bar z = a - bi its conjugate
  • a^2 + b^2 = \lvert z\rvert^2 — the (real, positive) squared modulus that ends up in the denominator

Example: for z = 3 + 4i,

\frac{1}{3 + 4i} = \frac{3 - 4i}{3^2 + 4^2} = \frac{3}{25} - \frac{4}{25}i.

Board: multiplicative inverse. For z = a + bi \neq 0, the inverse z^{-1} satisfies z z^{-1} = 1, and z^{-1} = \frac{1}{z} = \frac{1}{a + bi} \cdot \frac{a - bi}{a - bi} = \frac{a - bi}{a^2 + b^2} = \frac{\bar z}{\lvert z\rvert^2}. Check for the example: (3 + 4i)\left(\frac{3}{25} - \frac{4}{25}i\right) = 1.

Division in Cartesian form. For z_1 = a + bi and z_2 = c + di \ne 0,

\frac{z_1}{z_2} = \frac{a + bi}{c + di} = \frac{(a + bi)(c - di)}{c^2 + d^2} = \frac{ac + bd}{c^2 + d^2} + \frac{bc - ad}{c^2 + d^2}\,i.
Symbols
  • z_1 = a + bi — numerator; z_2 = c + di \ne 0 — denominator; a, b, c, d \in \mathbb{R}
  • c - di = \bar z_2 — conjugate of the denominator, by which numerator and denominator are multiplied
  • c^2 + d^2 = \lvert z_2\rvert^2 — the real denominator that results

Multiply by the conjugate of the denominator.

Worked example (slide 13). Compute \dfrac{3 + 4i}{1 + 2i}. Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate 1 - 2i:

\frac{3 + 4i}{1 + 2i} \cdot \frac{1 - 2i}{1 - 2i} = \frac{(3 + 4i)(1 - 2i)}{1^2 + 2^2} = \frac{11 - 2i}{5} = \frac{11}{5} - \frac{2}{5}i.

(Symbols as in the division formula above.)

Worked example — division step by step

Compute \dfrac{2 - 3i}{4 + i}.

  1. Find the conjugate of the denominator: \overline{4 + i} = 4 - i.
  2. Multiply top and bottom by it (this multiplies by 1, so the value doesn't change): \dfrac{(2 - 3i)(4 - i)}{(4 + i)(4 - i)}.
  3. Denominator becomes real: (4 + i)(4 - i) = 4^2 + 1^2 = 17.
  4. Expand the numerator, replacing i^2 by -1: 8 - 2i - 12i + 3i^2 = 8 - 14i - 3 = 5 - 14i.
  5. Split into real and imaginary part: \dfrac{5}{17} - \dfrac{14}{17}i.

Check: \left(\frac{5}{17} - \frac{14}{17}i\right)(4 + i) = \frac{20 + 5i - 56i - 14i^2}{17} = \frac{34 - 51i}{17} = 2 - 3i ✓.

Polar coordinates

The polar coordinate system is a two-dimensional coordinate system in which a point is determined by

  • a distance r from a reference point (the pole, usually the origin);
  • an angle \varphi from a reference direction (usually the positive x-axis).

P = (r, \varphi), with r \ge 0. (The slide's sketch shows P = (x, y) at distance r and angle \varphi, with x = r\cos\varphi and y = r\sin\varphi marked on the axes.)

Curves in polar coordinates

Circle r = 2, cardioid r = 1 + \cos\varphi, four-petal rose r = 2\cos(2\varphi), spiral r = \varphi/4.

The same shape may have a much shorter equation in polar coordinates.

Board. Examples: circle r = 1; rose curves r = a\cos(n\varphi), e.g. r = 2\cos(2\varphi): four-petal rose. The same curve can have different descriptions in Cartesian and polar coordinates.

Intuition

A polar equation says "at angle \varphi, go out a distance r". The circle r = 2 ignores the angle completely; in Cartesian form it needs x^2 + y^2 = 4. The spiral r = \varphi/4 moves outwards as the angle grows, which has no simple Cartesian equation at all.

Polar form of a complex number

Let z = x + yi correspond to a point with polar coordinates (r, \varphi):

x = r\cos\varphi, \qquad y = r\sin\varphi, \qquad r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = \lvert z\rvert.

Therefore

z = r(\cos\varphi + i\sin\varphi).
Symbols
  • x = \operatorname{Re} z, y = \operatorname{Im} z — Cartesian coordinates of z
  • r = \lvert z\rvert \ge 0 — the modulus: distance from z to 0
  • \varphi — the argument \arg z: angle from the positive real axis to z, in radians (or degrees), measured anticlockwise

Modulus r: distance from z to 0. Argument \varphi: angle from the positive real axis. Angles differing by 2\pi describe the same nonzero number.

Board. r = \lvert z\rvert \ge 0, \varphi = \arg z. The angle is not unique: \varphi + 2\pi k, k \in \mathbb{Z}, is also an argument when z \neq 0. A common choice of principal argument is \varphi \in (-\pi, \pi]. Engineering notation: z = r\angle\varphi.

Intuition — why a principal argument

Every nonzero z has infinitely many arguments (\frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{9\pi}{4}, -\frac{7\pi}{4}, … for 1 + i). To give the answer, one fixes a window of length 2\pi that contains each direction exactly once; with (-\pi, \pi], points above the real axis get positive angles, points below get negative ones, and the negative real axis gets \pi. The number 0 has no argument at all (r = 0, any angle gives the same point).

Intuition — two ways to give directions

Cartesian form says "go x east, then y north". Polar form says "face direction \varphi, then walk r". Same point, different instructions. Cartesian is natural for adding (add the east and north parts), polar for multiplying (see below). Converting between them is a core skill of this chapter.

Example: Cartesian → polar

Let z = 3 + 4i. Then r = \lvert z\rvert = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5. Since z lies in the first quadrant, \varphi = \arctan\frac{4}{3} \approx 53.1^\circ. Therefore

z = 5(\cos 53.1^\circ + i\sin 53.1^\circ).

(Symbols as above.) Always check the quadrant when using an inverse tangent.

Board: finding the modulus and argument.

  • Example 1: z = 3 + 4i: r = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5, \tan\varphi = \frac43. Since z is in the first quadrant, \varphi \approx 53.13^\circ, and z = 5(\cos 53.13^\circ + i\sin 53.13^\circ).
  • Example 2: z_1 = 1 + i: r_1 = \sqrt2, \varphi_1 = \frac{\pi}{4}.
  • Example 3: z_2 = -1 - i: r_2 = \sqrt2, \varphi_2 = \frac{5\pi}{4} = -\frac{3\pi}{4} \pmod{2\pi}.

Important: \tan\varphi = y/x alone does not identify the quadrant.

Board: another polar-form example. z = 1 + \sqrt3\,i: r = \sqrt{1^2 + (\sqrt3)^2} = 2, \cos\varphi = \frac12, \sin\varphi = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}, so \varphi = \frac{\pi}{3} and z = 2\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{3} + i\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\right).

Intuition — let cosine and sine pick the quadrant

Examples 2 and 3 have the same ratio y/x = 1, so \tan\varphi = 1 can't tell 1 + i from -1 - i. The board's last example avoids the problem: computing \cos\varphi = x/r and \sin\varphi = y/r separately fixes the signs of both coordinates, hence the quadrant. For -1 - i: \cos\varphi = \sin\varphi = -\frac{1}{\sqrt2}, both negative → third quadrant → \frac{5\pi}{4} (or -\frac{3\pi}{4}).

Common mistake — trusting \arctan(y/x) blindly

\arctan only returns angles between -90^\circ and 90^\circ, i.e. points to the right of the imaginary axis. For z = -1 + i (second quadrant), \arctan\frac{1}{-1} = -45^\circ points to 1 - i, the opposite direction. The right argument is -45^\circ + 180^\circ = 135^\circ = \frac{3\pi}{4}. Rule: if x < 0, add 180^\circ (\pi) to the arctan result. Always sketch the point first; the picture tells you the quadrant instantly.

Quick check: polar → Cartesian

Convert z = 2\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{3} + i\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\right) to Cartesian form. With \cos\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac12 and \sin\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}:

z = 1 + \sqrt3\,i.

Euler's formula

For every real \varphi,

e^{i\varphi} = \cos\varphi + i\sin\varphi.

So the polar form becomes

z = re^{i\varphi}.
Symbols
  • e \approx 2.718 — Euler's number, the base of the natural exponential
  • \varphi — a real angle in radians
  • e^{i\varphi} — the point on the unit circle (\lvert e^{i\varphi}\rvert = 1) at angle \varphi
  • r = \lvert z\rvert, \varphi = \arg z — as in the polar form

Board: three forms of a complex number. For z = x + iy, r = \lvert z\rvert, \varphi = \arg z:

  • Cartesian (algebraic): z = x + iy,
  • Polar (trigonometric): z = r(\cos\varphi + i\sin\varphi),
  • Euler (exponential): z = re^{i\varphi}.

At \varphi = \pi: e^{i\pi} = \cos\pi + i\sin\pi = -1. Hence Euler's identity:

e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0.

(Symbols as above.)

Intuition — why an exponential?

The point of writing e^{i\varphi} is that it obeys the exponential rule e^{i\alpha}e^{i\beta} = e^{i(\alpha + \beta)} (shown in the next section): multiplying such numbers adds their angles, just as e^a e^b = e^{a+b} adds exponents. The lecture takes the formula as given; proving it needs power series, which come later in analysis. Mind the units: the angle must be in radians, so e^{i\pi} = -1 but "e^{i \cdot 180}" is not.

Multiplication and division in polar form

Write z_j = r_j(\cos\varphi_j + i\sin\varphi_j), j = 1, 2. Then

z_1 z_2 = r_1 r_2\big(\cos(\varphi_1 + \varphi_2) + i\sin(\varphi_1 + \varphi_2)\big).

By Euler's formula this is just

z_1 z_2 = r_1 r_2\,e^{i(\varphi_1 + \varphi_2)}.
Symbols
  • z_1, z_2 — the two factors; j = 1, 2 numbers them
  • r_1, r_2 — their moduli; \varphi_1, \varphi_2 — their arguments (radians)
  • r_1 r_2 — modulus of the product; \varphi_1 + \varphi_2 — argument of the product

Multiply the magnitudes: r_1 r_2. Add the angles: \varphi_1 + \varphi_2. For example, multiplication by i is a 90^\circ anticlockwise rotation.

Why do the angles add?

Multiply out with the Cartesian rule: (\cos\varphi_1 + i\sin\varphi_1)(\cos\varphi_2 + i\sin\varphi_2) = (\cos\varphi_1\cos\varphi_2 - \sin\varphi_1\sin\varphi_2) + i(\sin\varphi_1\cos\varphi_2 + \cos\varphi_1\sin\varphi_2). The real part is exactly the addition formula for \cos(\varphi_1 + \varphi_2), the imaginary part the one for \sin(\varphi_1 + \varphi_2). So the product of two unit-circle numbers is the unit-circle number at the summed angle; the factors r_1, r_2 just come along and multiply. The trig addition formulas you once memorised are complex multiplication in disguise.

For z_j as above with z_2 \ne 0:

\frac{z_1}{z_2} = \frac{r_1}{r_2}\big(\cos(\varphi_1 - \varphi_2) + i\sin(\varphi_1 - \varphi_2)\big), \qquad \text{equivalently} \qquad \frac{z_1}{z_2} = \frac{r_1}{r_2}\,e^{i(\varphi_1 - \varphi_2)}.
Symbols
  • z_1 — numerator, z_2 \ne 0 — denominator, so r_2 > 0
  • r_1/r_2 — modulus of the quotient; \varphi_1 - \varphi_2 — argument of the quotient

Divide the magnitudes: r_1/r_2. Subtract the angles: \varphi_1 - \varphi_2. The AC-circuit example uses this formula directly.

Board. Multiplication: multiply moduli and add arguments. Division: divide moduli and subtract arguments. In angle notation: \dfrac{6\angle 40^\circ}{2\angle 10^\circ} = 3\angle 30^\circ.

Worked example — multiplying in polar form

z_1 = 2e^{i\pi/6}, z_2 = 3e^{i\pi/3}.

  1. Multiply the moduli: 2 \cdot 3 = 6.
  2. Add the arguments: \frac{\pi}{6} + \frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\pi}{2}.
  3. Write the result and convert if needed: z_1 z_2 = 6e^{i\pi/2} = 6(\cos\frac{\pi}{2} + i\sin\frac{\pi}{2}) = 6i.

In Cartesian form the same product would be (\sqrt3 + i)\left(\frac32 + \frac{3\sqrt3}{2}i\right): four terms and square roots, for the same 6i.

Connection

Multiplying by e^{i\varphi} rotates the plane by \varphi, which is what the rotation matrix \begin{pmatrix}\cos\varphi & -\sin\varphi \\ \sin\varphi & \cos\varphi\end{pmatrix} from 2.2 Matrices and Transformations does to vectors. Complex numbers are a compact way to do 2D rotations; robotics uses this for planar robot poses.

Powers and roots

Binomial expansion: the motivation

The binomial theorem gives, for n \in \mathbb{N},

(a + b)^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} a^{n-k} b^k, \qquad \binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}.
Symbols
  • a, b — any (real or complex) numbers; n \in \mathbb{N} — the power
  • \sum_{k=0}^{n} — sum over k = 0, 1, \dots, n
  • \binom{n}{k} — binomial coefficient, "n choose k"; n! = 1 \cdot 2 \cdots n (with 0! = 1)

Let u = \cos\varphi + i\sin\varphi. For n = 2:

\begin{aligned} u^2 &= \cos^2\varphi + 2i\sin\varphi\cos\varphi + i^2\sin^2\varphi \\ &= (\cos^2\varphi - \sin^2\varphi) + i(2\sin\varphi\cos\varphi) \\ &= \cos(2\varphi) + i\sin(2\varphi). \end{aligned}
Symbols
  • u — a complex number on the unit circle at angle \varphi
  • the last step uses the double-angle formulas \cos 2\varphi = \cos^2\varphi - \sin^2\varphi and \sin 2\varphi = 2\sin\varphi\cos\varphi

It looks like multiplying the angle by 2; does a general pattern exist?

Board. Similarly, u^3 = \cos 3\varphi + i\sin 3\varphi.

Powers: De Moivre's formula

For n \in \mathbb{N},

\big(r(\cos\varphi + i\sin\varphi)\big)^n = r^n(\cos n\varphi + i\sin n\varphi), \qquad \text{equivalently} \qquad (re^{i\varphi})^n = r^n e^{in\varphi}.
Symbols
  • r \ge 0, \varphi — modulus and argument of the base
  • n \in \mathbb{N} — the exponent
  • r^n — modulus of the power; n\varphi — argument of the power

Example: (\cos 30^\circ + i\sin 30^\circ)^6 = \cos 180^\circ + i\sin 180^\circ = -1.

Board: the same example in radians. \left(\cos\frac{\pi}{6} + i\sin\frac{\pi}{6}\right)^6 = \cos\left(6 \cdot \frac{\pi}{6}\right) + i\sin\left(6 \cdot \frac{\pi}{6}\right) = \cos\pi + i\sin\pi = -1. In exponential notation: \left(e^{i\pi/6}\right)^6 = e^{i\pi} = -1.

Board: proof by induction (outline). Base case n = 1 is clear. Assume z^k = r^k(\cos k\varphi + i\sin k\varphi). Multiply by z = r(\cos\varphi + i\sin\varphi): z^{k+1} = r^{k+1}\big(\cos((k+1)\varphi) + i\sin((k+1)\varphi)\big). Use the angle-addition identities. The claim follows by induction.

Why does De Moivre's formula hold?

It is the polar multiplication rule applied n times: each multiplication by re^{i\varphi} multiplies the modulus by r and adds \varphi to the angle. After n factors: modulus r^n, angle n\varphi. Formally, by induction on n (see 1 Elements of Logic): true for n = 1; if (re^{i\varphi})^n = r^n e^{in\varphi}, then (re^{i\varphi})^{n+1} = r^n e^{in\varphi} \cdot re^{i\varphi} = r^{n+1}e^{i(n+1)\varphi}.

Worked example — a high power without expanding

Compute (\sqrt3 + i)^6.

  1. Convert to polar: r = \sqrt{3 + 1} = 2; the point is in the first quadrant, \varphi = \arctan\frac{1}{\sqrt3} = \frac{\pi}{6}.
  2. Apply De Moivre: (2e^{i\pi/6})^6 = 2^6 e^{i\pi} = 64e^{i\pi}.
  3. Convert back: e^{i\pi} = -1, so (\sqrt3 + i)^6 = -64.

The binomial theorem would need 7 terms with powers of \sqrt3 and i.

n-th roots in polar form

Let z = r(\cos\varphi + i\sin\varphi) with r > 0. To solve w^n = z:

w_k = \sqrt[n]{r}\left(\cos\frac{\varphi + 2k\pi}{n} + i\sin\frac{\varphi + 2k\pi}{n}\right), \qquad k = 0, \dots, n-1,

equivalently w_k = r^{1/n} e^{i(\varphi + 2k\pi)/n}.

Symbols
  • z — the given number, with modulus r > 0 and argument \varphi
  • n \in \mathbb{N} — the order of the root; w — the unknown
  • w_k — the k-th root, k = 0, 1, \dots, n - 1
  • \sqrt[n]{r} = r^{1/n} — the ordinary positive real n-th root of r
  • All roots have modulus \sqrt[n]{r}.
  • Their angles are separated by 2\pi/n.
  • They form the vertices of a regular n-gon.

Board: how many solutions? The equation x^4 = 1 has 2 real solutions, 1 and -1, but 4 complex solutions: 1, -1, i, -i. For z \neq 0, w^n = z has exactly n distinct solutions in \mathbb{C}. Derivation: write z = r(\cos\varphi + i\sin\varphi), r > 0, and w = \rho(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta). By De Moivre's formula, w^n = z means \rho^n = r, n\theta = \varphi + 2\pi k; therefore w_k = \sqrt[n]{r}\left(\cos\frac{\varphi + 2\pi k}{n} + i\sin\frac{\varphi + 2\pi k}{n}\right), k = 0, 1, \dots, n - 1.

Why are there exactly n roots, and where does the 2k\pi come from?

By De Moivre, w = \rho e^{i\theta} satisfies w^n = \rho^n e^{in\theta}. For this to equal re^{i\varphi} we need \rho^n = r (so \rho = \sqrt[n]{r}) and n\theta to be the same direction as \varphi, i.e. n\theta = \varphi + 2k\pi for some integer k, because angles differing by 2\pi give the same number. So \theta = \frac{\varphi + 2k\pi}{n}. Dividing by n turns the 2\pi ambiguity into steps of \frac{2\pi}{n}: k = 0, \dots, n - 1 give n different directions, and k = n brings you back to k = 0.

Example: cube roots of 1

Solve w^3 = 1 = e^{i \cdot 0}. The three roots are

w_k = e^{2\pi k i/3}, \quad k = 0, 1, 2: \qquad 1, \quad -\frac12 + \frac{\sqrt3}{2}i, \quad -\frac12 - \frac{\sqrt3}{2}i.

(Symbols as in the root formula, with r = 1, \varphi = 0, n = 3.)

The three cube roots of 1 on the unit circle, 120^\circ apart.

Board. For w^3 = 1: r = 1 and \varphi = 0, so w_k = \cos\frac{2\pi k}{3} + i\sin\frac{2\pi k}{3}: w_0 = \cos 0 + i\sin 0 = 1, w_1 = \cos\frac{2\pi}{3} + i\sin\frac{2\pi}{3} = -\frac12 + \frac{\sqrt3}{2}i, w_2 = \cos\frac{4\pi}{3} + i\sin\frac{4\pi}{3} = -\frac12 - \frac{\sqrt3}{2}i. Second example: w^4 = 1: w_0 = 1, w_1 = i, w_2 = -1, w_3 = -i.

Worked example — fourth roots of -16

Solve w^4 = -16.

  1. Write the right side in polar form: -16 has modulus 16 and lies on the negative real axis: -16 = 16e^{i\pi}.
  2. Modulus of the roots: \sqrt[4]{16} = 2.
  3. Angles: \frac{\pi + 2k\pi}{4} for k = 0, 1, 2, 3: \frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{3\pi}{4}, \frac{5\pi}{4}, \frac{7\pi}{4}, spaced by \frac{2\pi}{4} = 90^\circ.
  4. Convert: 2e^{i\pi/4} = \sqrt2 + \sqrt2 i, and the others are -\sqrt2 + \sqrt2 i, -\sqrt2 - \sqrt2 i, \sqrt2 - \sqrt2 i: a square.

Check one: (\sqrt2 + \sqrt2 i)^2 = 2 + 4i - 2 = 4i, and (4i)^2 = -16 ✓.

Common mistake — only one root, or real-number root rules

Over \mathbb{R}, "\sqrt{\ }" means one specific root, and rules like \sqrt{ab} = \sqrt a\sqrt b hold for a, b \ge 0. Over \mathbb{C}, w^n = z always has n solutions, and stopping at the first one (k = 0) loses the rest. The real-number rules also break: \sqrt{-4}\cdot\sqrt{-9} = 2i \cdot 3i = -6, not \sqrt{36} = 6. Work with the polar root formula and list all k.

Applications

AC circuits and phase

A sinusoidal voltage can be represented by a complex phasor. Suppose

\tilde V = 10\angle 0^\circ\ \mathrm{V}

and the circuit impedance is

Z = 3 + 4i\ \Omega = 5\angle 53.1^\circ\ \Omega.

Ohm's law becomes

\tilde I = \frac{\tilde V}{Z} = 2\angle(-53.1^\circ)\ \mathrm{A}.
Symbols
  • \tilde V — voltage phasor: amplitude (V) and phase angle of a sinusoidal voltage, in one complex number
  • Z — impedance (Ω): the complex "resistance" of the circuit; real part = resistance, imaginary part = reactance
  • \tilde I — current phasor: amplitude (A) and phase of the resulting current
  • \angle\theta — shorthand for polar form: A\angle\theta = Ae^{i\theta}, modulus A, argument \theta

One division gives both current magnitude and phase shift.

The same example in the complex plane: \tilde V on the real axis, \tilde I rotated by -53.1^\circ.

Impedance Z = 3 + 4i: \lvert Z\rvert = 5, \arg Z = 53.1^\circ. Current: \tilde I = \frac{10}{5}e^{-i53.1^\circ} = 2e^{-i53.1^\circ}.

In electrical engineering the imaginary unit is often written j, because i is used for current.

Board: where the phasor comes from. A sinusoidal voltage v(t) = V_0\cos(\omega t + \varphi_v), where V_0 is the amplitude, \omega the angular frequency, and \varphi_v the phase, has the voltage phasor \hat V = V_0 e^{i\varphi_v} = V_0\angle\varphi_v. Example: \hat V = 10\angle 0^\circ V. With the complex impedance \hat V = Z\hat I, Z = 3 + 4i\ \Omega = 5\angle 53.13^\circ\ \Omega: \hat I = \dfrac{10\angle 0^\circ}{5\angle 53.13^\circ} = 2\angle(-53.13^\circ) A. The current lags the voltage by 53.13^\circ: i(t) = 2\cos(\omega t - 53.13^\circ) A.

Symbols
  • v(t) — voltage at time t (V); i(t) — current at time t (A; here i is the current, not the imaginary unit)
  • V_0 — amplitude (peak voltage, V); \omega — angular frequency (rad/s); \varphi_v — phase angle of the voltage
  • \hat V, \hat I — voltage and current phasors (the board's hat notation; the slide writes \tilde V, \tilde I)
  • Z — impedance (Ω)
Why can the time dependence \omega t be dropped from the phasor?

In a circuit driven at one frequency \omega, every voltage and current oscillates with that same \omega; they differ only in amplitude and phase. The phasor stores exactly these two numbers, and v(t) is recovered as the real part of \hat V e^{i\omega t} = V_0 e^{i(\omega t + \varphi_v)}, whose real part is V_0\cos(\omega t + \varphi_v) by Euler's formula. Dividing phasors divides amplitudes and subtracts phases, which is the 2\angle(-53.13^\circ) result: amplitude 10/5 = 2 A, phase 0^\circ - 53.13^\circ.

Intuition — what the -53.1^\circ means

The current has amplitude 2\,\mathrm{A} (that's 10/5, the polar division of moduli) and lags the voltage by 53.1^\circ: its peaks come a bit later than the voltage's. A pure resistor would give a real Z and no shift; the 4i part (here an inductance) causes the lag. Without complex numbers you'd have to solve a differential equation to find both numbers; with them it's one division.

Sound and Fourier analysis

A complicated sound signal can be decomposed into sinusoidal components. Each frequency component has

  • an amplitude;
  • a phase.

These two quantities fit naturally into one complex number. A Fourier transform tells us which frequencies are present and with what complex amplitudes. This is used in

  • audio filtering;
  • communications;
  • image processing.

Complex numbers are a language for oscillations.

Connection

The sinusoids A\sin(\omega t + \varphi) from 4 Oscillations and Waves are exactly what one complex amplitude Ae^{i\varphi} encodes. Fourier analysis returns in 9 Measurement and Signal Processing (Introduction to Robotics).

Fundamental theorem of algebra

Every non-constant polynomial with complex coefficients has at least one complex root.

Equivalently, a degree-n polynomial has exactly n complex roots when multiplicities are counted:

p(z) = a_n(z - z_1)(z - z_2)\cdots(z - z_n), \qquad a_n \ne 0.
Symbols
  • p(z) — a polynomial of degree n in the complex variable z
  • a_n \ne 0 — its leading coefficient (the coefficient of z^n)
  • z_1, \dots, z_n — its roots, possibly repeated

Over \mathbb{C}, polynomial factorisation into linear factors is complete.

Intuition

Over \mathbb{R}, z^2 + 1 cannot be factored further; over \mathbb{C} it splits as (z - i)(z + i). The theorem says this never fails again: once complex numbers are allowed, no new numbers are needed to solve polynomial equations. For a real quadratic with negative discriminant, the two roots come as a conjugate pair: z^2 + 2z + 5 = 0 gives z = \frac{-2 \pm \sqrt{4 - 20}}{2} = -1 \pm 2i.

Roots and multiplicity

If

p(z) = (z - z_0)^k q(z), \qquad q(z_0) \ne 0,

then z_0 is a root of multiplicity k.

Symbols
  • z_0 — a root of the polynomial p
  • k \in \mathbb{N} — its multiplicity: how many times the factor (z - z_0) appears
  • q(z) — the remaining polynomial, which does not vanish at z_0 (so no further factor (z - z_0) hides in it)

Example: p(z) = z^3 + 2z^2 - 7z + 4 = (z + 4)(z - 1)^2. So -4 is a simple root, and 1 has multiplicity 2.

Board: polynomial division for this example. p(z) = z^3 + 2z^2 - 7z + 4. Since p(1) = 1 + 2 - 7 + 4 = 0, z_1 = 1 is a root. If z_1 is a root, then p(z) = (z - z_1)g(z) with g(z) = \dfrac{p(z)}{z - z_1}. Long division:

stepsubtractremainder so far
z^3 \div z = z^2z^2(z - 1) = z^3 - z^23z^2 - 7z + 4
3z^2 \div z = 3z3z(z - 1) = 3z^2 - 3z-4z + 4
-4z \div z = -4-4(z - 1) = -4z + 40

So p(z) = (z - 1)(z^2 + 3z - 4). Now solve z^2 + 3z - 4 = 0: \Delta = 9 + 16 = 25, z_{2,3} = \frac{-3 \pm 5}{2} = 1, -4. Hence p(z) = (z - 1)^2(z + 4). Roots: 1 of multiplicity 2; -4 of multiplicity 1.

Intuition — why a root gives a factor

Dividing p(z) by (z - z_1) always leaves a remainder that is a constant c: p(z) = (z - z_1)g(z) + c. Put in z = z_1: p(z_1) = 0 \cdot g(z_1) + c = c. So the remainder is exactly p(z_1), and it is 0 precisely when z_1 is a root. That is why one guessed root lets you split off a linear factor and continue with a polynomial of lower degree, as in the table.

Worked example — counting roots with multiplicity

p(z) = z^3 - 4z^2 + 5z - 2.

  1. Guess a root among the divisors of the constant term (\pm1, \pm2): p(1) = 1 - 4 + 5 - 2 = 0 ✓.
  2. Divide out (z - 1): z^3 - 4z^2 + 5z - 2 = (z - 1)(z^2 - 3z + 2).
  3. Factor the quadratic: z^2 - 3z + 2 = (z - 1)(z - 2).
  4. Collect: p(z) = (z - 1)^2(z - 2). Roots: 1 with multiplicity 2, 2 simple. Total 2 + 1 = 3 = \deg p ✓, as the theorem promises.

Optional: \mathbb{C} as an algebraic structure

RingField
A set with addition and multiplication satisfying the usual algebraic rules, including additive inverses and distributivity.A commutative ring in which every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse.
Example: \mathbb{Z} is a ring.Examples: \mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{R}, \mathbb{C} are fields.

This language explains why arithmetic works similarly in \mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{R} and \mathbb{C}.

Common mistake — comparing complex numbers

\mathbb{R} is an ordered field (3 Set of Real Numbers); \mathbb{C} is a field but not ordered. "2 + i < 3i" has no meaning, and there is no way to define < on \mathbb{C} that keeps the usual rules (if i > 0, then i \cdot i = -1 > 0; if i < 0, then (-i)(-i) = -1 > 0; both contradict 1 > 0). Inequalities in complex problems always compare real quantities, such as moduli: \lvert z_1\rvert < \lvert z_2\rvert is fine.

Quick check

For z = 1 - \sqrt3\,i, find \bar z, \lvert z\rvert, one argument of z, and the polar form.

  • \bar z = 1 + \sqrt3\,i
  • \lvert z\rvert = 2
  • \arg z = -\frac{\pi}{3}
  • z = 2e^{-i\pi/3}

Board: polar form of a point below the real axis. Take z = 1 - \sqrt3\,i. Its modulus is r = \sqrt{1 + 3} = 2. Its argument can be chosen as \varphi = -\frac{\pi}{3}. Therefore z = 2\left(\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{3}\right) + i\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\right) = 2e^{-i\pi/3}.

Key Facts

Cartesian form

  • z = a + bi, i^2 = -1
  • \operatorname{Re} z = a, \operatorname{Im} z = b
  • (a + bi)(c + di) = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i

Conjugate and modulus

  • \bar z = a - bi, \lvert z\rvert = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}
  • z\bar z = \lvert z\rvert^2
  • \frac{1}{z} = \frac{\bar z}{\lvert z\rvert^2}, z \ne 0

Polar form

  • z = r(\cos\varphi + i\sin\varphi) = re^{i\varphi}
  • z_1 z_2 = r_1 r_2 e^{i(\varphi_1 + \varphi_2)}
  • \frac{z_1}{z_2} = \frac{r_1}{r_2}e^{i(\varphi_1 - \varphi_2)}

Powers, roots, polynomials

  • (re^{i\varphi})^n = r^n e^{in\varphi}
  • n-th roots are equally spaced on a circle
  • Every degree-n polynomial has n complex roots, counting multiplicity.
